content: Diphtheritic stomatitis is a recently identified disease that has, to date, been observed exclusively in Yellow-eyed penguins (Megadyptes antipodes). The clinical presentation of this condition bears similarities to human diphtheria and is characterized by infectious lesions in the oral cavity. These lesions interfere with the ability to swallow and can lead to respiratory complications. The causative agent of this disease is Corynebacterium amycolatum, an aerobic, Gram-positive bacterium. The infection predominantly affects very young chicks. It is hypothesized that another factor, such as a viral co-infection, may play a role in predisposing the penguins to this condition, rendering the Corynebacterium a secondary pathogen. This disease has been a significant cause of mortality during the Yellow-eyed penguin breeding seasons of 2002 and 2004. The outbreaks appear to have been geographically limited to the South Island of New Zealand and Stewart Island/Rakiura. Clinical Signs and Symptoms The disease is almost exclusively observed in Yellow-eyed penguin chicks. Affected individuals exhibit labored breathing and signs of general weakness. Yellow, caseous exudate is present within the beak and at the commissures of the mouth. A yellow diphtheritic membrane often covers the hard palate, tongue, and buccal mucosa. In severe cases, the lesions prevent the mouth from closing, and the tongue may remain exposed. Diagnosis Diagnosis can be confirmed by isolating Corynebacterium amycolatum from clinical specimens. Alternatively, histopathological examination can reveal findings consistent with diphtheria. Treatment During the 2004 outbreak, various treatment strategies were trialed. The primary approach involved the administration of antibiotics. In some cases, additional supportive care, such as glucose solutions or dietary supplements, was provided. The outcomes of these treatment methods varied significantly. The efficacy of antibiotic therapy, as well as the feasibility of its widespread application in wild animal populations, remains a topic of ongoing debate.
